title: Peppermint humbugs
subtitle: traditional striped pulled sugar sweets with a strong peppermint flavour
excerpt: Peppermint humbugs are a traditional British boiled sweet made by pulling a batch of hard sugar syrup while it is still warm to incorporate air and lighten its colour, then twisting a darker and a lighter strand together to make the classic stripe. The process requires two people and confidence working with hot sugar.
sourceNotes: Peppermint humbugs are a traditional British boiled sweet documented in Victorian confectionery manuals. Method from Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) and later British confectionery sources.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sugar cooking stage reached at 149 to 154°C, at which the syrup sets rigid and brittle when cooled. Used for boiled sweets, toffee, and pulled sugar work.
A technique in which sugar syrup cooked to the hard crack stage is stretched and folded repeatedly while warm to incorporate air, making it opaque and silky.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 3 weeks. Wrap individually in waxed paper or twist wrappers.
recipe.temperatureNote: hard crack stage (150 to 154°C on a sugar thermometer)

content.text: . The pulling stage, done while the sugar is still warm enough to stretch, incorporates air and makes the sugar opaque. A small portion is coloured dark (traditionally with a little black food colouring or treacle) and twisted with the light pulled portion to create the stripe. This is best done with two people: one to pull and one to hold the hook or post.
Sugar syrup at hard crack stage is around 150°C. Serious burns are a real risk. Wear heat-resistant gloves when pulling, keep children away from the work area, and have cold water nearby.

items.prepNote: enough to colour a small portion dark (or use 1 tsp black treacle)

content.text: Put the sugar, golden syrup, water, and cream of tartar into a heavy-based saucepan. Heat over a low heat, stirring, until the sugar has dissolved. Bring to the boil and cook without stirring until the thermometer reads 150 to 154°C.
Remove from the heat and stir in the peppermint extract. Pour two-thirds of the mixture onto a lightly oiled marble or silicone mat and set the remaining third aside in the pan.

When the large portion is cool enough to handle (it will feel very warm but should hold its shape when folded), begin pulling: stretch it out, fold it back on itself, and repeat over a hook or the back of a clean wooden spoon. Continue for 5 to 8 minutes until the sugar becomes opaque and satin-like.
Colour the remaining third in the pan with black food colouring or black treacle. Stir to combine. Pour onto the mat next to the pulled portion.

Lay the dark strand alongside the pulled light strand and twist them together, then roll into a long rope about 1 cm in diameter. Cut into 2 cm pieces with oiled scissors before the sugar fully hardens.
Leave on a silicone mat to cool completely for 30 to 60 minutes, until fully hard. Store immediately in an airtight tin.

attrs.problem: Sugar hardens before pulling is complete
attrs.avoid: Avoid waiting too long before starting the pull; work in a warm kitchen and begin pulling as soon as you can handle the sugar safely.
attrs.fix: You can briefly warm the sugar on a very low heat if it sets too early, but the texture will not be as good. Work faster next time.

attrs.problem: Humbugs stick together in the tin
attrs.avoid: Avoid storing without individual wrappers in a humid environment.
attrs.fix: Wrap each sweet in a small square of waxed paper and store in a well-sealed tin.
